cards.term: What does Theseus think of the lovers' story of the night?
cards.def: He finds it "more strange than true," saying he never may believe "these antique fables, nor these fairy toys," because lovers and madmen "apprehend more than cool reason ever comprehends."

cards.term: Which three figures does Theseus say "are of imagination all compact"?
cards.def: "The lunatic, the lover, and the poet": the madman sees more devils than hell can hold, the lover sees Helen's beauty in "a brow of Egypt," and the poet's pen gives "to airy nothing / A local habitation and a name."

cards.term: What everyday fear does Theseus use to illustrate imagination's tricks?
cards.def: He says that at night, "imagining some fear, / How easy is a bush suppos'd a bear!"

cards.term: How does Hippolyta answer Theseus's skepticism?
cards.def: She says that all the story of the night, and all their minds "transfigur'd so together," "more witnesseth than fancy's images, / And grows to something of great constancy."

cards.term: How much time must Theseus fill, and whom does he call to manage the entertainment?
cards.def: He wants masques, dances, or a play "to wear away this long age of three hours / Between our after-supper and bed-time," and he calls Philostrate, "our usual manager of mirth."

cards.term: Which three entertainments does Theseus reject, and why?
cards.def: He rejects the battle with the Centaurs, already told to Hippolyta "in glory of my kinsman Hercules"; the riot of the tipsy Bacchanals tearing Orpheus, an "old device"; and the "thrice three Muses mourning," a "satire keen and critical, / Not sorting with a nuptial ceremony."

cards.term: What contradictions does Theseus find in the description of Pyramus and Thisbe?
cards.def: The paper calls it "a tedious brief scene" of "very tragical mirth," which he compares to "hot ice and wonderous strange snow," asking how they will "find the concord of this discord."

cards.term: Why does Philostrate try to stop the play, and why does Theseus hear it anyway?
cards.def: Philostrate says it is "ten words" too long, with "not one word apt, one player fitted," and that he shed "merry tears" at the rehearsal, but Theseus answers, "never anything can be amiss, / When simpleness and duty tender it."

cards.term: What is wrong with Quince's prologue, according to the court?
cards.def: Because he pauses at the wrong places, he seems to say the opposite of what he means; Theseus says "this fellow doth not stand upon points," and Lysander adds that "it is not enough to speak, but to speak true."

cards.term: Who plays which part in the mechanicals' show?
cards.def: Quince speaks the Prologue; Bottom plays Pyramus; Flute plays Thisbe; Snout presents Wall with loam and a cranny of fingers; Starveling presents Moonshine with lanthorn, dog, and bush of thorn; and Snug plays Lion.

cards.term: What plot does the Prologue already tell before the acting begins?
cards.def: Pyramus and Thisbe whisper through Wall's chink, plan to meet at Ninus's tomb by moonshine, Thisbe is affrighted by a lion and drops her mantle, Pyramus finds it bloodstained and stabs himself, and Thisbe then kills herself with his dagger.

cards.term: What mixed-up senses and names appear in the wall scene?
cards.def: Pyramus says, "I see a voice" and hopes to "hear my Thisby's face"; he compares himself to "Limander" and "Shafalus," Thisbe answers "Helen" and "Procrus," and they agree to meet at "Ninny's tomb."

cards.term: How does Snug try to keep the ladies from fearing the lion?
cards.def: He addresses "you, ladies, you, whose gentle hearts do fear / The smallest monstrous mouse," then says, "I, one Snug the joiner, am / A lion-fell, nor else no lion's dam."

cards.term: What happens at "old Ninny's tomb"?
cards.def: Thisbe arrives, the lion roars and she runs off dropping her mantle, the lion tears the mantle, Pyramus finds it "stain'd with blood" and stabs himself, and Thisbe returns, mourns him, and stabs herself.

cards.term: What does Theseus mean by "the best in this kind are but shadows"?
cards.def: He tells Hippolyta, who calls the play "the silliest stuff that ever I heard," that even the best plays are only shadows, "and the worst are no worse, if imagination amend them."

cards.term: What offer does Bottom make after the lovers die, and what does Theseus choose?
cards.def: Bottom, no longer "dead," offers "the epilogue, or to hear a Bergomask dance between two of our company"; Theseus says the play "needs no excuse" and asks for the Bergomask, telling them to "let your epilogue alone."

cards.term: What time is it when the dance ends, and how long will the revels continue?
cards.def: "The iron tongue of midnight hath told twelve," Theseus says "'tis almost fairy time," and he promises, "A fortnight hold we this solemnity, / In nightly revels, and new jollity."

cards.term: In this edition, what happens in Act 5, Scene 2 before Puck's last speech?
cards.def: Puck enters with a broom "to sweep the dust behind the door," then Oberon and Titania lead the fairies in song and dance to bless the palace.

cards.term: What blessing does Oberon give the three wedding couples?
cards.def: He and Titania will bless "the best bride-bed" so that "the issue there create / Ever shall be fortunate," the three couples shall "ever true in loving be," and no mole, hare-lip, scar, or "mark prodigious" shall be on their children.

cards.term: How does Puck ask the audience to take the play if it has offended them?
cards.def: He says, "If we shadows have offended, / Think but this, and all is mended, / That you have but slumber'd here / While these visions did appear," and that the "weak and idle theme" is "no more yielding but a dream."

cards.term: What does Puck ask for in his final couplet?
cards.def: "Give me your hands, if we be friends, / And Robin shall restore amends."

cards.term: What literary device is "very tragical mirth" or "hot ice"?
cards.def: It is an oxymoron, the conjunction of normally incompatible terms, which Theseus also hears in "tedious" and "brief."

cards.term: How is the mechanicals' play a parody of tragedy?
cards.def: It uses the conventions of a tragic love-death, including a lion, a bloody mantle, apostrophes to Night and the Fates, and double suicide, but the bungled verse, mixed senses, and broken character turn the catastrophe into farce.

cards.term: Why is the court audience's knowledge of the actors an example of dramatic irony?
cards.def: The spectators, and we, already know that Lion is Snug, Wall is Snout, and Pyramus is Bottom, so every claim that the lion is dangerous or that Pyramus is really dying is the opposite of what we know.
